results.content: The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) Background The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), related to the design effect (DEFF) [1] as: DEFF = 1 + (n − 1)ICC is a key parameter in the design and analysis of group- or cluster-randomized trials (GRTs or CRTs). The ICC, together with the degrees of freedom (df) based on the number of groups or clusters, is commonly used to calculate how much the sample size of a CRT should be inflated compared with a simple individual-randomized trial. [2] provide a general definition of the ICC as a common correlation coefficient between responses of any two subjects from the same cluster. results.title: The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient in Mixed Models
results.content: # The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient in Mixed Models The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, or ICC, can be very useful in many statistical situations, but especially so in Linear Mixed Models. Linear Mixed Models are used when there is some sort of clustering in the data. Mixed models not only account for the correlations among observations in the same cluster, they give you an estimate of that correlation. If there is no real correlation among observations within a cluster, the cluster means won’t differ. If you find that the correlation is zero, that means the observations within clusters are no more similar than observations from different clusters. 3. results.title: What is an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)? - StatsTips
results.content: # StatsTips. What is an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)? # What is an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)? ##### statstips Comments 0 Comment. In biostatistics, the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) measures the reliability or consistency of measurements made by different observers or instruments for the same subject. One of the more commonly accepted classifications for deciding the type of ICC to perform is **Shrout and Fleiss’s Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) classification. It** is a widely-used framework introduced in their 1979 paper, providing a detailed system for choosing the appropriate type of ICC based on the study design. **Shrout and Fleiss’s Classification for ICC**. Shrout and Fleiss proposed **three models** of ICC, each suited for different study designs. These models are based on whether raters or subjects are treated as random or fixed effects and whether you are interested in measuring absolute agreement or consistency between raters. 1. **ICC Model 1: One-way Random Effects Model (ICC(1))**. * **Use Case**: This model is appropriate when a random sample of raters rates different subject**s**, and each subject is rated by a **different set of raters**. 1. **ICC Model 2: Two-way Random Effects Model (ICC(2))**. * **ICC(2,1)**: Assesses the **absolute agreement** between individual raters. * **ICC(2,k)**: Assesses the **absolute agreement** between the **average of k raters**. 1. **ICC Model 3: Two-way Mixed Effects Model (ICC(3))**. This model is appropriate when you are only interested in the reliability of these specific raters. Unlike ICC(2), it does not account for random variance from raters, as raters are treated as fixed. * **ICC(3,1)**: Assesses **consistency** of ratings from individual raters. 1. **One-way random effects (ICC(1))**: Use when a different set of raters rates each subject, and those raters are a random sample from a larger pool. * **ICC(1)**: One-way random effects for independent raters,. * **ICC(2)**: Two-way random effects for the same raters, with results generalizable to other raters,. * **ICC(3)**: Two-way mixed effects for the same fixed raters without generalization. results.title: Human biomarker interpretation: the importance of intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) and their calculations based on mixed models, ANOVA, and variance estimates - PMC
results.content: # Human biomarker interpretation: the importance of intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) and their calculations based on mixed models, ANOVA, and variance estimates. In the first section, the history and philosophical aspects of interpreting repeat measures of biomarkers via ICC calculations are presented starting with early efforts from the 1950s for assessing occupational exposures and health and then continuing on to the present with applications for assessing environmental exposures and preclinical adverse health effects and estimating long-term latency risks. The second section reviews methods for calculating ICC parameters, demonstrates how synthetic data might be constructed to test such methods, and reviews the different data structures that may be encountered in human biomarker measurements studies. In this section, a few methods for calculating ICC from biomonitoring data with repeat measures are described and evaluated. For the relatively simple application of repeat analysis interpretation encountered in environmental and biological measurements research, techniques are based on analysis of variance (ANOVA) statistics or restricted maximum likelihood to calculate the between-sample variance (σb2) and within-sample variance (σb2) to calculate ICC as:. (2014) found instances when variance calculations, ANOVA, or mixed-model estimates result in negative ICC; this is recognized as a statistical artifact most likely due to data outliers, especially when the true ICC is very close to 0 and the repeat measures are highly random. It is of utmost importance to understand that robust ICC calculations require that the underlying data are normally distributed and that the repeat measures also represent homogeneity of variance; as such, it is generally required to calculate ICC using log-transformed data as real-world measurements tend to start off as lognormally distributed (Pleil et al. The basic premise is that the measurement values and their distributions reflect real-world data but that the number of repeat measures, the within-and between-subject variance components, and the internal data configurations such as ICC, repeat measures, missing values or total samples are manipulated to generalize the results to a variety of generic possibilities.
